title: Why did England ban Indian cotton?
teaches: India's lead in fine spinning and fast printed cotton; Indian cloth as the currency of the spice trade; monsoon trade cycles; the East India Company; consumer demand and the industrious revolution; the Calico Acts of 1700 and 1721 and their loopholes

blocks.text: In June 1719 several thousand silk weavers from Spitalfields, in east London, marched through the streets attacking women who were wearing printed cotton. They tore gowns off their wearers' backs and threw ink and acid on others. The attacks went on, on and off, for more than a year, and pamphlets on both sides argued about whether a woman in a calico gown was a traitor to English workers. The weavers' complaint was simple: fashionable people had stopped buying the silks and woollens they made and were wearing cheap, bright, washable cotton imported from India.

In 1721 Parliament gave the weavers most of what they wanted. It became illegal in Britain to wear or use printed or dyed cotton cloth, with a fine for the wearer and a larger one for the seller. In this lesson we look at why Indian cotton was so popular that a government banned it: what India could make that Europe could not, how the trade worked, and how the ban was designed in a way that later helped British cotton manufacturing grow.

For about two thousand years before 1800, the Indian subcontinent made more cotton cloth, and finer cotton cloth, than anywhere else. Lesson 3 described Bengal's hand spinners, who spun yarn fine enough for muslins that Europe could not match. Lesson 5 described how Indian dyers used mordants and resists to put several fast colours on cotton. Gujarat, the Coromandel coast in the southeast and Bengal in the east each had their own kinds of cloth, made by millions of spinners, weavers, bleachers, printers and dyers, most working in villages and paid for each piece.

Indian cloth was sold all round the Indian Ocean: in East Africa, Arabia, Persia and Southeast Asia. In the spice islands of what is now Indonesia, it was the main thing traders could buy spices with. When Dutch and English merchants arrived there around 1600 with silver, they found that the people who grew pepper, cloves and nutmeg wanted Indian cottons more than silver. The Dutch and English companies therefore set up trading posts on the Indian coast to buy cloth, and used it to pay for spices. One estimate, by the economic historian Paul Bairoch, puts India's share of the world's manufacturing output in 1750 at about a quarter; the figure is rough, and some historians think it too high, but no one disputes that India was then one of the world's great industrial regions.

A printed or painted cotton was the result of many stages of work. The **hours bar** below estimates them for a length of fine chintz, the painted and printed cotton Europeans most wanted, using the arithmetic of lesson 3.

blocks.text: Spinning was most of the work, as it was for the Viking sail, and it was done mostly by women at home. Weavers, bleachers and printers were usually paid by merchants who advanced them money months ahead against the cloth they would deliver. Labour was cheap, but this was still about a year's work for one person, so chintz was not cheap to make. It was cheap compared with the silks and fine woollens it replaced, because European cloth of similar quality took similar hours at much higher wages.

Trade across the Indian Ocean ran on the **monsoon**, the seasonal reversal of the winds. From about November to March the wind blows from the northeast, off the land, and ships could sail west from India towards Arabia and East Africa. From about June to September it blows from the southwest, bringing the rains, and ships sailed the other way; in its first, stormiest months most ports on India's west coast closed. Ships could sail against the wind only slowly and at great risk, so a voyage had to wait for the right season.

blocks.text: The wind calendar decided how long a merchant's money was tied up. Cloth was bought months before the ship sailed, with advances to weavers; then it waited for its wind, sailed, was sold, and the proceeds came home on the next season's wind. A merchant who missed the season lost most of a year. That made Indian Ocean trade a business for people with capital who could afford to wait, and it is one reason the European companies, with large pools of shareholders' money, could grow inside it.

parts.title: The Company and the calico craze

blocks.text: The English **East India Company**, chartered in 1600, came to India for spices and pepper and found that cloth sold better in Europe than anyone expected. Cotton was light and washable, it took colours that did not run, and printed chintz came in patterns that could be changed every season. The Company sent English designs to India for Indian printers to copy and adapt to European taste. By the 1680s it was shipping more than a million pieces of cotton cloth to England in some years, much of it re-exported to Europe, West Africa and the American colonies.

The buyers were not only the rich. The historian Jan de Vries has argued that from the late 17th century, households in northwestern Europe worked more hours for wages, and sent more of their members out to work, in order to buy goods such as cottons, sugar, tea and tobacco. He called this the **industrious revolution**, a rise in demand that came before the machines of the Industrial Revolution. Cheap, bright, washable Indian cotton was one of the things people worked for.

The silk and wool industries fought back. France banned imported and home-printed cottons outright in 1686, and the ban lasted until 1759, although smuggling made it hard to enforce. England's first **Calico Act**, in 1700, banned imports of printed, painted and dyed cotton from India, Persia and China. It left a loophole: plain white Indian calico could still be imported, and English printers began printing it in London. The riots of 1719 and 1720 pushed Parliament further, and the Act of 1721 banned wearing printed or dyed cotton altogether.

The 1721 Act had its own exceptions. Muslins, neckcloths, blue-dyed calico and, above all, **fustians**, the cloth with a linen warp and a cotton weft from lesson 9, remained legal. Lancashire made fustians, and its makers argued successfully, in an Act of 1736, that printed fustian was not calico. So the law that shut out Indian cotton protected a British cloth that was part cotton. British manufacturers then needed only one thing to replace Indian cloth entirely: cotton yarn strong enough for the warp. Lessons 14 and 15 follow the machines that made it. In 1774 Parliament lifted the ban for cotton cloth spun and woven in Britain, after a campaign by Richard Arkwright and his partners, whose water frame spun such a yarn and who wanted to sell all-cotton cloth.

**Try it.** Lesson 5 dipped a whole cloth in alum. Indian dyers painted it on in a pattern. Stir a teaspoon of alum into a few tablespoons of flour paste, paint a pattern onto white cotton with it, let it dry, dye the whole piece in strong onion-skin dye, then rinse well. The pattern stays darker where the alum was. Painting two different mordants on one cloth, then dyeing once, gives two colours: that is the principle of Indian chintz.

blocks.caption: Five questions on Indian cotton and the calico bans.

items.ask: Dutch traders in the spice islands around 1600 found that silver did not buy as many spices as they hoped. What did they do?
choices: Bought Indian cloth and traded it for spices
Brought Dutch woollens to trade instead
Planted their own spices in Holland
Paid the growers in gold coins
items.why: Indian cloth was the currency the spice growers wanted, so the European companies had to buy into the Indian cloth trade to reach the spices.

items.ask: A Gujarati merchant misses the sailing season for the Red Sea by a month. What does it cost him?
choices: Most of a year, waiting for the next season's wind
About a month, until the next ship sails
Nothing; ships could sail whenever they liked
Only the cost of storing the ship in port
items.why: Each leg could be sailed only in its monsoon season, so a missed season meant waiting months with capital tied up.

items.ask: The 1700 Calico Act banned printed Indian cotton but allowed white calico. What happened?
choices: English printers printed white calico in London
Calico disappeared from English shops
Indian printers moved to London to work
English wool sales tripled within a year
items.why: The loophole created an English printing industry on Indian cloth, which is one reason the riots and the 1721 Act followed.

items.ask: Why did the 1721 ban end up helping Lancashire?
choices: It shielded Lancashire's fustian from Indian cloth
It paid Lancashire's weavers a yearly subsidy
It banned wool, so buyers turned to cotton
It moved the East India Company to Manchester
items.why: Fustian was exempt, so a British cotton-linen industry grew behind the ban. It needed only a strong cotton warp yarn to make all-cotton cloth.

items.ask: Jan de Vries's industrious revolution says demand grew before the machines. What is the evidence of it in this lesson?
choices: Ordinary households bought so much cotton that weavers rioted
Factories were built in India to meet European demand
Cotton prices rose sharply as supply failed to keep up
Only the rich could afford to wear Indian cotton
items.why: The calico craze reached far down the social scale. Households worked more for wages to buy goods like cotton, which created a market before British machines could supply it.

summary: **India led the world in cotton.** Its spinners made the finest yarn and its dyers the fastest colours on cotton, for markets all round the Indian Ocean.
**Indian cloth bought spices.** In Southeast Asia it worked as currency, so the European companies had to buy cloth in India first.
**Spinning was most of the work.** Even fine chintz took more hours at the spinning wheel and spindle than at the loom or the dye vat.
**The monsoon set the calendar.** Ships sailed each leg only in its season, so capital was tied up for most of a year.
**Europeans wanted cotton.** By the 1680s the East India Company shipped over a million pieces a year in some years, printed to European taste.
**Demand came first.** The industrious revolution describes households working more to buy goods like cotton.
**Silk and wool weavers fought back.** France banned calicoes from 1686 to 1759; England's Acts of 1700 and 1721 banned printed Indian cotton and then its wearing.
**The bans had loopholes.** White calico was printed in London, and fustian was protected, which helped Lancashire's part-cotton industry grow.
**The ban ended in 1774.** British machines could by then spin cotton strong enough for an all-cotton cloth.
